title: Identifying reference to abstract objects in dialogue
research_question: Can linguistically naive annotators reliably identify unconstrained stretches of prior dialogue that serve as antecedents for discourse-deictic references to abstract objects?
methodology: The authors conducted two annotation experiments on TRAINS-91 task-oriented planning dialogues using MMAX2. In the first experiment, 20 paid native-English-speaking undergraduates were trained to mark arbitrary text regions as segment antecedents, with 19 completing the task; in the second, four previously trained participants used a coarser scheme in which antecedents were collections of utterances, with one participant excluded and an experimenter added to the analysis. Agreement was examined using majority patterns, antecedent-boundary comparisons, and Krippendorff alpha with several set-distance measures. Custom scripts propagated discourse-region antecedents through coreference chains before analysis.

key_findings.finding: Using a criterion of at least three annotators, 35 of 181 phrase markables in the first dialogue, or 19.3%, had a plausible discourse-segment antecedent; a similar 20 of 102, or 19.6%, was obtained in the second experiment after removal of an outlying annotator.

Annotators showed meaningful but far from perfect convergence on antecedent spans: for the 16 most readily identified anaphors, Krippendorff alpha was 0.45 with Jaccard distance and 0.55 with both Dice and Passonneau distances.

Antecedent endings were more consistently localized than antecedent beginnings; among the 16 clearest cases, annotators chose the most popular beginning 42% of the time and the most popular ending 64% of the time.
Demonstrative pronouns, especially 'that', were much more readily associated with discourse-segment antecedents than personal 'it' or suggestive definite descriptions.

A simple model based on selecting an antecedent at a fixed distance from the anaphor explained much of the annotators' span behavior, suggesting that approximate antecedent vicinity may be easier to identify than exact boundaries.

Some discourse-deictic references depend on several preceding utterances and admit distinct abstract interpretations; the authors' example of 'is that correct' shows that a text-span annotation can identify the relevant prior region without distinguishing whether the referent is a plan or a fact about the plan.
The authors explicitly caution that annotation by third-party overhearers may yield lower agreement than the understanding achieved by actual dialogue participants during grounding.

limitations: Both experiments use only a very small number of dialogues from the TRAINS-91 planning domain, where references to plans are unusually frequent.
The second experiment has very few annotators; one of four participants was excluded and an experimenter was added as an annotator.
Arbitrary span boundaries are intrinsically difficult, with substantially more disagreement about where an antecedent starts than where it ends.
The text-region method cannot distinguish fine semantic alternatives such as reference to a plan versus reference to a fact about the plan.
Some agreement statistics are difficult to interpret because expected distances can become extremely large relative to local span-boundary disagreement.
A simple distance-based baseline accounts for much of human boundary placement, limiting evidence that detailed human span annotation adds substantial information beyond antecedent vicinity.
Annotators are overhearers rather than dialogue participants and lack the grounding context available to the original speakers.
The study concerns abstract reference rather than explicit question-answer alignment and therefore does not directly label partial answers or unanswered questions.
The custom Perl processing scripts and resulting experimental annotations are described but not reported as publicly released artifacts.
raw_claims: The experiments ask annotators to identify prior regions of dialogue associated with references to abstract objects.
Roughly one fifth of the evaluated markables met the authors' criterion for a plausible discourse-segment antecedent in each experiment.
Different annotators often selected overlapping rather than exactly identical antecedent spans.
Agreement was noticeably stronger for the end boundary of a discourse antecedent than for its beginning.
Demonstrative forms were much more likely than personal 'it' to receive discourse-segment antecedents.
The most consistently identified segment-anaphoric expressions in the first experiment were demonstratives referring largely to plans.
Coarser utterance-based annotation simplified the annotation task but did not remove interpretive ambiguity.
A discourse-deictic expression may package several preceding utterances into one abstract referent.
Text-span agreement alone cannot always establish which abstract semantic object the speaker intended.
A simple locality model reproduces a substantial amount of annotator behavior.
